meta: Mushfiq's Persian miniature of Zulaykha in her palace and as an old woman with Joseph, from a copy of Jami's Five Treasures, 1603 to 1607.
about: Zulaykha appears four times in this Persian miniature. Twice she is in wall murals, once she sits in the palace above, and below she bows as an old woman in a blue veil toward Joseph, who wears a golden halo. The Cleveland Museum of Art says a golden pot of white narcissus at the bottom center signals that her youth and beauty are about to be restored. In this Persian retelling of the Bible story, Zulaykha lusted after Joseph although she was married to Potiphar. Joseph resisted her until she became a widow.
credit_line: Gift in honor of Madeline Neves Clapp; Gift of Mrs. Henry White Cannon by exchange; Bequest of Louise T. Cooper; Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund; From the Catherine and Ralph Benkaim Collection

meta: Vincent van Gogh's Farmhouse in Provence, 1888, sold through Julien Tanguy and later bequeathed by Ailsa Mellon Bruce.
about: A sunlit farmhouse with orange-tiled roofs stands behind a low stone wall and a blue gate, with haystacks rising in a golden wheat field. A man in a blue jacket walks along the path at left. In November 1890 Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, the artist's sister-in-law, sold it through Julien Tanguy's gallery in Paris to Willy Gretor. Gretor gave it to the painter Maria Slavona, and her husband Otto Ackermann also owned it. Gaston Bernheim de Villers had it by 1919. Captain Edward Molyneux sold it in 1955 to Ailsa Mellon Bruce, who left it to the National Gallery of Art.

meta: Eugène Delacroix's 1838 Christopher Columbus and His Son at La Rábida, painted for Prince Anatoly Demidov near Florence.
about: Monks in dark and cream habits talk in an arched corridor while a bearded man in a red doublet sits nearby and another figure rests on a bench beside a staff and a bundle. Anatoly Demidov, prince of San Donato, commissioned the picture. Félix Bracquemond etched it for the catalogue of Demidov's sale in Paris in 1870, where Edouard André bought it for 38,000 francs. It sold again in London for 30,187 francs. Peter A.B. Widener of Philadelphia owned it later. Chester Dale bought it in 1932 and left it to the National Gallery of Art.

meta: Jean Honoré Fragonard's Love as Folly, about 1773 to 1776, a cherub with a ribbon among doves, made as a pair with Love the Sentinel.
about: A winged cherub with rosy skin and a pink drapery holds a flowing pink ribbon above a cloud and a garden of roses. Three white doves glide through the pale sky above him, and two more rest at the lower left. The painting has a pendant, Love the Sentinel, also in the National Gallery. Georges Wildenstein later wrote that his father bought the pair from the marquis des Isnards, whose family held an unwritten tradition that they had owned both since they were painted. John Woodruff Simpson of New York bought Love as Folly in 1905 or 1906. His daughter Jean W. Simpson gave it in 1947.
credit_line: In memory of Kate Seney Simpson

meta: Paul Gauguin's 1888 Breton Girls Dancing, Pont-Aven, acquired from the artist by the dealers Boussod, Valadon the same year.
about: Three young women in Breton dress, with white lace headdresses and collars, dance hand in hand in a grassy field. Haystacks and a dog are nearby, and a village with a church spire lies behind a stone wall. Boussod, Valadon and Company acquired the painting from Gauguin in November 1888. A buyer named Montandon bought it the next year. The dealer Ambroise Vollard held it for years afterward. After the estate sale of William A. Cargill in Scotland, a Paris dealer bought it for Paul Mellon, who gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1983.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Thomas Gainsborough's Mrs. John Taylor, about 1778, painted for her husband in Birmingham and later owned by Andrew W. Mellon.
about: A woman with powdered grey hair piled high turns her head slightly to the left with a soft smile. Her white dress is trimmed with pearls at the neckline and sleeves and tied with a pale blue sash. Gainsborough painted the oval portrait for her husband, John Taylor of Bordesley Park and Moseley Hall near Birmingham. It passed down to George W. Taylor, who still owned it when it was shown at Birmingham in 1903. It then went through dealers in Paris and New York to Andrew W. Mellon. Mellon's charitable trust gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1937.

meta: Albert Besnard's double portrait of Madeleine Lerolle and her daughter Yvonne, about 1879 to 1880, set in a studio.
about: A woman in a black dress and feathered hat sits beside a young girl in a white lace-trimmed dress who leans against her. Albert Besnard was a good friend of the artist Henri Lerolle, whose wife Madeleine and daughter Yvonne are the sitters. Large portfolios of drawings at lower right and an easel at upper left point to the profession of the painter. The easel holds a canvas tipped forward at an unusual angle, and the Cleveland Museum of Art explains that it has been strapped there so the artist can paint more easily while seated.
credit_line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Noah L. Butkin

meta: William Adolphe Bouguereau's Rest, 1879, bought from the artist by the Cleveland banker Hinman B. Hurlbut.
about: A woman sits beneath trees with a curly-haired toddler on her lap, while an older boy sleeps barefoot on the grass in front of them. In the distance a domed building rises in the haze. The Cleveland Museum of Art says the dome of Saint Peter's stresses the moral virtues of the Italian peasants. Their idealized figures and triangular grouping recall Raphael's Holy Family paintings from 400 years earlier. Hinman B. Hurlbut, a banker and philanthropist in Cleveland, bought the painting directly from the artist in July 1879.

meta: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi's scroll of the lord Kenshin writing a poem under a full moon, from the series Twelve Aspects of the Moon.
about: A seated warrior in armor, a white headcloth and a green robe gazes up at a pale full moon while a line of geese flies across the misty sky. He is the lord Uesugi no Terutora, known as Kenshin, in his military encampment beside a banquet for his generals. The Art Institute of Chicago says he is enjoying a moment of quiet before the next day's battle against his longtime rival. The geese passing the moon move him to write a poem. Christie's in New York sold the scroll in 2007 to Roger Weston of Chicago, who gave it to the museum in 2018.

meta: Tao Hong's 1633 hanging scroll Clouds Visiting a Mountain Retreat, the largest of only five known works by him.
about: Mist covers a mountain that rises above gnarled pines, and a path leads toward a small walled dwelling. Two figures cross a wooden bridge at the lower left. The Cleveland Museum of Art says little is known about Tao Hong, who settled in Nanking late in life. His son was a friend of the Nanjing school artist Gong Xian. When the Ming dynasty collapsed in 1644, Tao joined the loyalist resistance in Yunnan. By 1645 the Manchu invaders had defeated the Yunnanese forces, and Tao fled to Burma, where he died shortly afterward. Only five of his works survive. This is the largest.
credit_line: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund

meta: John Constable's Cloud Study: Stormy Sunset, 1821 to 1822, which came down through his granddaughter before the National Gallery of Art bought it in 1998.
about: A broad sky fills this oil sketch, with heavy dark grey clouds tinged with rose above a pale, sunlit land. Patches of pale blue sky break through the clouds. The study belonged to the artist's granddaughter, Ella Mackinnon, and then to Sir Henry Newson-Smith. His son Sir Frank Newson-Smith sold it at Christie's in London in 1951 as A Stormy Sunset. After passing through a private collection and a New York gallery, it was bought by the National Gallery of Art in 1998.
credit_line: Gift of Louise Mellon in honor of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Hendrick Goltzius's 1613 Vertumnus and Pomona, in which Vertumnus appears as an old woman.
about: Vertumnus has taken the shape of an old woman to speak to his beloved Pomona, who lies naked under an apple tree. Pomona holds a small pruning knife in her right hand, the tool she used to gather fruit. The old woman grasps a vine tendril, and a walking stick lies between her legs. Apples, pears and grapes are heaped at lower right. Goltzius signed the picture HG 1613.

meta: Jan Steen's The Quack, about 1650, a village scene of a charlatan showing off a tooth he has pulled.
about: On a village square, a quack stands on a platform under a big tree and shows the villagers the tooth, or stone, that he has drawn from a man tied to a chair. A basket of eggs stands at the patient's feet. The table holds bottles, small pots and a sealed document. At the right in the foreground a woman pushes her drunken husband away in a wheelbarrow. Farther right a fiddle hangs from a pole where a monkey sits with a pipe. Steen signed the panel at lower left.

meta: Maarten van Heemskerck's 1529 portrait of a man counting money, once identified as the Amsterdam mint master Pieter Gerritsz Bicker.
about: A man sits half-length behind a table counting money, an open book in his left hand. On the table lie a stamp, a stick of wax and a ball of string, and a mirror hangs on the wall. The Rijksmuseum notes that he was formerly identified as Pieter Gerritsz Bicker, mint master and alderman of Amsterdam. The picture has a pendant, and the title suggests that it shows his wife, possibly Anna Codde.

meta: Claude-Joseph Vernet's A Calm at a Mediterranean Port, 1770, a harbor at sunset with fishermen cleaning their catch.
about: Fishermen clean the day's catch on a stone pier while several people chat nearby, and one of them points toward the large ship in the bay. A man sits smoking a pipe. The tobacco glows bright red. A cumulus cloud, perhaps the remnant of a distant storm, towers to the left of the setting sun. The Getty says warm yellow, orange and red tones suggest a hazy sunset after a bright day. A tall lighthouse on a fortified base stands at the left.

meta: Gustave Courbet's The Black Rocks at Trouville, 1865 to 1866, once owned by Mary Cassatt.
about: Rust-red and dusky clouds fill the upper part of the picture above a calm, pale sea. Dark weathered rocks lie along the low shoreline in the foreground, and two small sailboats drift near the horizon. The first owner on record is the American painter Mary Cassatt, though the museum notes the picture may instead have belonged to a Cassatt family collection and not to her personally. Wildenstein in London acquired it in 1943, and in 1950 it went to a private collection in Buenos Aires. The National Gallery of Art bought it in 2011.

meta: Paul Klee's graphic score of the opening bars of Bach's Adagio from his sixth violin sonata, from the Bauhaus lectures behind The Thinking Eye.
about: A handwritten page of musical notation shows Klee's graphic version of the opening bars of the Adagio from Bach's sixth sonata for violin and obbligato harpsichord. The top staff has notes and rests, and the lower staves carry black filled bars with German notes such as Erstes Achtel. This is the beginning of a fold-out. It comes from Klee's Bauhaus lectures of 1921 and 1922, which were published as The Thinking Eye in his Pedagogical Notebooks. Bach's piece is catalogued as BWV 1019.

meta: Marie Bracquemond's The Backgammon Players, shown at the last Impressionist exhibition in 1886 and acquired by the Clark in 2024.
about: Two women in light dresses sit on an oriental rug beside a pond and play backgammon, each holding a small cup. A pitcher and a dish rest on the grass. The French catalog text says the picture was shown at the last Impressionist exhibition in 1886 and was probably painted a few years earlier, soon after the couple settled at Sèvres. The subject comes straight from walks in the nearby Bois de Saint-Cloud and shows two elegant women outdoors by a stream, absorbed in a popular table game. It stayed with the artist's family until a sale in Paris, and the Clark Art Institute acquired it in 2024.

meta: Honoré Daumier's In Church, about 1855 to 1857, lent to a Daumier exhibition in Paris in 1901 and given to the National Gallery of Art in 1943.
about: Two women in white bonnets sit pressed together in profile, with a third figure half hidden in shadow at the right. The brushwork is loose and sketchy, and the palette is a dark brown. Daumier initialed the panel h.D. at lower left. The collector Carabin lent it to a Daumier exhibition in Paris in 1901. The dealer Charles Sessler of Philadelphia sold it to Lessing J. Rosenwald on 30 June 1930, according to Sessler's records, though the bill of sale is dated the next day. Rosenwald gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1943.

meta: Paul Cézanne's Landscape near Paris, about 1876, once in the collection of Egisto Fabbri in Florence and later owned by Chester Dale.
about: A dirt path crosses a sunlit open field toward a cluster of low buildings with red tiled roofs, and two leafy green trees rise at the center. The brushwork is loose and feathery. Egisto Fabbri of Florence probably acquired the painting from the dealer Ambroise Vollard and still had it in 1920. Paul Rosenberg's gallery sold it in November 1927 to Chester Dale of New York. Dale gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1963.

meta: Jean-Louis Forain's The Races at Longchamp, about 1891, later owned by Paul Mellon.
about: Spectators in top hats and elaborate period dresses crowd a racecourse, and some stand on chairs to see the race. Jockeys on horses gallop across the grass in the distance. Forain signed it at lower right. The painting was with a collector recorded as Tchoukin at the turn of the century, and Durand-Ruel in Paris and New York handled it later. By 1926 it belonged to Thorsten Laurin in Stockholm. Paul Mellon left it to the National Gallery of Art in 1999, with a life interest for his wife Rachel Lambert Mellon.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Winslow Homer's The Red School House, 1873, bought by Paul Mellon in 1970 and given to the National Gallery of Art.
about: A young woman in a striped dress and white bonnet stands in the foreground holding a book, with a red schoolhouse and a few small figures behind her under a pink and yellow evening sky. Homer signed and dated the picture at lower right and scratched the same signature and date into the paint at upper right before painting over them. Nellie Taylor of Boston is reported to have said that her father bought it directly from Homer. Paul Mellon bought it from E.V. Thaw and Company in 1970 and gave it to the National Gallery in 1985.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Katsukawa Shunsho's hanging scroll of women and a boy airing books and clothes in summer to guard against mildew and insects.
about: Four women and a young boy lay out paper-covered books taken from protective cabinets. The books hang over a line to air. The National Museum of Asian Art explains that books and clothing were aired each summer to prevent mildew and insects. One woman has stopped working. She is distracted by what she has found in an open book. A cuckoo flies across the top of the scroll, and the museum says the bird is often linked with courtesans or with poems of love and longing.

meta: Jan van Goyen's 1646 View of Rhenen, a river landscape that reached the National Gallery of Art in 2014 from the Corcoran Gallery.
about: A tall church tower rises above a town on the right of a broad river landscape, and windmills stand along the distant rise. In the foreground a horse-drawn carriage and several walkers travel a dirt road beside marshy ground. Goyen signed it with his name and the date at lower right. Dr. Abraham Bredius of Amsterdam and Sir George Donaldson of London owned it at one time. William A. Clark of New York bought it in 1906 and bequeathed it to the Corcoran Gallery of Art. The National Gallery of Art acquired it from the Corcoran in 2014.

meta: Edgar Degas's Alexander and Bucephalus, 1861 to 1862, a youth approaching a horse, sold from his studio in 1918 under a different title.
about: A young figure in a white tunic and blue cloak approaches a chestnut horse beside a red drape, while onlookers in dark and colored robes watch from the right. The picture appeared in the first sale of Degas's studio in Paris in 1918 as Achilles and Bucephalus. Dr. Hans Graber, an art historian and collector in Morcote, owned it by 1951. The dealers Knoedler and Pinakos handled it later, and Lore Heinemann of New York bequeathed it to the National Gallery of Art in 1997.
credit_line: Bequest of Lore Heinemann in memory of her husband, Dr. Rudolf J. Heinemann

meta: Lucas Cranach the Elder's Madonna and Child, probably about 1535 or later, marked with the artist's winged serpent device.
about: A half-length Madonna in red and teal robes with an orange mantle holds a bunch of grapes, and the nude infant Christ standing on a table reaches for one. A glass of pale wine and an apple rest on the stone ledge in front. Above the Madonna's shoulder at upper right is Cranach's device, a serpent with folded wings. The gallery's provenance notes list the H. Michels Gallery in Berlin as a probable early owner, with Van Diemen and Company in New York showing it in 1929. Adolph Caspar Miller of Washington owned it by 1937. It came to the National Gallery of Art as a gift in 1953.

meta: George Catlin's A Small Cheyenne Village, 1861 to 1869, which passed from his daughters to the American Museum of Natural History.
about: An oval painting shows a small camp of conical tipis on open grassland beneath rolling green hills, with a mounted rider and several figures moving among the lodges. Trees line the left edge. George Catlin kept the picture himself, and it passed to his three daughters, Clara, Louise and Elizabeth. The American Museum of Natural History bought it in 1912 from Elizabeth Wing Catlin. Kennedy Galleries in New York sold it in 1959 to Paul Mellon, who gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1965.

meta: John Singleton Copley's portrait of Harrison Gray, about 1767, which passed down in the Otis family.
about: A man in a powdered white wig and a rust-brown coat with gold buttons and braid sits holding a quill pen and a sheet of paper against a deep green background. It probably went from the sitter to his daughter Elizabeth Gray Otis and then to her son Harrison Gray Otis. From him it passed through four more generations of the Otis family. The last owner, William Alleyne Otis of Boston, was succeeded by his cousins Robert and Virginia Thayer of Washington, who gave the portrait to the National Gallery of Art in 1976.
credit_line: Gift of the Honorable and Mrs. Robert H. Thayer

meta: Henri Fantin-Latour's 1866 Still Life of pears, apples and camellias, later owned by Chester Dale.
about: A wicker basket of pears, apples and a quince stands beside a dark blue vase of pink and white camellias. A peeled orange, a whole orange and a teacup on a saucer rest on a red tray. Fantin-Latour signed and dated it at upper right. Reginald Davis of Paris owned the picture before it was sold at the Hôtel Drouot in 1909. After A.T. Hollingsworth of London sold it at Christie's in 1929, the dealers Reid and Lefevre and Knoedler shared it, and Chester Dale bought it that June through Galerie Bignou. Dale bequeathed it to the National Gallery of Art.

meta: Mary Cassatt's Little Girl in a Blue Armchair, 1878, bought from the artist by Ambroise Vollard and later given by Paul Mellon.
about: A young girl in a white lace-trimmed dress and tartan sash reclines in a blue armchair with her arm behind her head. A small dark dog sleeps in a second blue armchair at the left. Ambroise Vollard bought the painting from Cassatt, and his name and address, M. Vollard, 6 Rue Lafitte, are penciled on the stretcher crossbar. Hector Brame in Paris sold it in November 1963 to Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon, who gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1983.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Gerrit Willem Dijsselhof's 1890 Meadow Landscape on the Spaarne, on loan to the Rijksmuseum from 1919 and bequeathed in 1944.
about: Cows graze in a flat meadow under a pale, cloudy sky, and a windmill stands at the water's edge in the distance. A line of trees runs along the right horizon, and a pale strip of water across the middle ground is the river Spaarne. In 1919 Jean Charles Joseph Drucker and Maria Lydia Drucker-Fraser of Montreux lent the painting to the Rijksmuseum with 70 other paintings. They bequeathed it to the museum in 1944, together with 71 others.

meta: Martin Schongauer's engraving Christ Before Pilate, from The Passion of Christ, with Pilate washing his hands.
about: Pilate sits on his high chair, a little left of center, and faces the viewer. He washes his hands in a basin that his servant holds at the left, while an attendant pours water from a ewer. At the right Christ stands bound in a crown of thorns, held by a group of soldiers. Two dogs lie in the foreground.

meta: Robert Jones's 1810 design for the north wall of the Yellow Drawing Room at the Royal Pavilion in Brighton.
about: This is a pencil elevation of a wall for the Yellow Drawing Room at the Royal Pavilion in Brighton. A large central panel of flowering plants and containers with flowers is flanked by two narrow panels of birds and plants. Their frames end at the top in cusped arches in the Indian style, and the museum says the whole decoration reflects that taste. Patterned lattice and an ornamental railing run below.

meta: Albrecht Dürer's Sixth Knot, from his Six Knots, a circular pattern of interlaced cords around his monogram.
about: On a black circular ground, a pattern of continuous knots forms six roundels with open centers around a seventh, and the seventh holds the artist's monogram. At the four corners of the plate, stylized black trees carry further knots and tendrils. The interlaced strands run in eight looped rings around the center.

meta: Giuseppe Barberi's 1770 pen and wash design for an oil lamp, with a semi-nude woman holding up a flaming brazier.
about: A round plinth with bands of acanthus decoration carries a column. On the column sits a semi-nude woman who holds a flaming brazier aloft in her left hand, and at her side Cupid stands on one foot with his quiver. The drawing is a design for an oil lamp, made in pen and brown wash. The brazier itself is a large ornamental bowl. Flames rise from its rim.

meta: Jean-Baptiste Pillement's title page for his New Series of Notebooks of Ideal Flowers, no. 3, made for designers and painters.
about: Two stems of fantastical leaves and blossoms in a gradient of color cross at the base and form a frame around the lettering. The French text announces a new series of notebooks of ideal flowers for the use of designers and for painters. It says Jean Pillement invented and drew them and that Anne Allen engraved them. Below it is the number 3. The wreath is oval, with fern-like fronds in red, green, blue, purple and brown.
